description: Operating solo for the 2026 sprint. I am combining frontend development, interactive data visualization, and rapid prototyping to build a clean, functional web application using NASA open datasets.
summary: MissionForge is a browser-based space engineering game that makes mission trade-offs playable. Players choose a science objective, configure a spacecraft and launch vehicle, balance budget, mass, power, storage and communications, then simulate operations and evaluate the science returned. Earth, Moon and Mars scenarios connect engineering choices to visible consequences: eclipses drain batteries, limited contacts restrict downlink, and full recorders lose observations. An explanatory debrief helps players revise and compare designs. Solo play and shared-device teams of up to four require no accounts or servers. NASA-derived planetary and atmosphere data support the wider flight and learning systems, while the studio clearly labels its simplified hardware and scoring assumptions.
details:
MissionForge — Project Details

Overview

MissionForge is an interactive, browser-based space mission design and engineering game created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 — Space Mission Design Game challenge.

The project transforms complex space engineering concepts into an engaging, educational experience where players design spacecraft, manage mission resources, simulate space operations, and learn how engineering decisions affect mission success.

Rather than simply launching a rocket or exploring planets, MissionForge allows players to understand the science behind their decisions through simulation, real NASA-derived data, and detailed mission feedback.

How MissionForge Works

The central feature is Mission Design Studio, where players design scientific missions involving Earth, the Moon, and Mars.

Players begin by selecting a scientific objective, such as conducting an Earth imaging survey, collecting lunar geological observations, or performing a Mars imaging mission.

They then configure their spacecraft and mission using several interconnected systems:

  • Spacecraft engineering: Select instruments, solar arrays, batteries, communication systems, data recorders, and launch vehicles.
  • Mission planning: Choose orbital parameters, mission duration, and available budget.
  • Resource management: Balance spacecraft mass, electricity generation, battery storage, communication capacity, and scientific data storage.
  • Mission simulation: Observe how eclipses, power shortages, communication limitations, and storage capacity affect scientific operations.
  • Mission evaluation: Review scientific data returned, mission costs, operational failures, and improvement opportunities.

During a simulation, spacecraft operations advance in one-minute intervals. Solar power generation varies with distance from the Sun, while planetary eclipses interrupt generation. Scientific instruments collect observations, onboard storage retains data, and communication opportunities determine how much information can be transmitted to Earth.

A critical learning principle is that collecting scientific observations does not automatically mean completing a successful science mission. Only observations successfully transmitted to Earth contribute to the mission's science score.

After each mission, players receive an explanatory debrief highlighting technical decisions, resource limitations, and opportunities for improvement.

Players can modify their designs, repeat missions, and compare results.

Additional Features

Beyond Mission Design Studio, MissionForge includes:

  • An interactive rocket builder with spacecraft components, staging, engineering calculations, and launch-readiness checks.
  • Playable rocket flight missions involving launch, orbital mechanics, and mission objectives.
  • Solar-system exploration with planetary environments, orbital maps, and spacecraft controls.
  • Mission Control Academy, which introduces orbital mechanics, propulsion, staging, and other spaceflight concepts.
  • NASA Data Explorer, which connects scientific reference values to planetary and flight calculations.
  • Optional advanced scientific and engineering simulation tools.
  • Local saving, design comparison, data export, and mission reports.
  • Single-player gameplay and shared-device collaboration for teams of up to four people.

MissionForge runs directly in a compatible web browser without requiring players to create accounts or use a dedicated gameplay server.

NASA Data Integration

MissionForge integrates scientific reference data derived from NASA resources, rather than simply displaying NASA information as background material.

The project uses archived information from NASA's General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT) and JPL/NAIF references, including:

  • Planetary dimensions and rotation parameters.
  • Gravitational parameters used in orbital calculations.
  • Earth and Mars atmospheric density reference tables.
  • Scientific constants and documented unit conversions.

These inputs support calculations involving planetary gravity, orbital velocity, orbital periods, and atmospheric effects.

NASA Data Explorer allows players to inspect sources, units, assumptions, and derived values.

The mission-design system also draws educational inspiration from NASA CubeSat 101 and the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook.

MissionForge is an independent educational project. Its simplified spacecraft hardware, budgets, communication schedules, and scoring systems are illustrative models, not actual NASA mission specifications.

Technology and Development

MissionForge was developed using:

  • JavaScript for game systems, simulations, and interactive functionality.
  • React 19 for the user interface and application architecture.
  • Three.js and WebGL for interactive 3D rendering.
  • HTML and CSS, including Tailwind CSS, for interface design and responsive layouts.
  • Node.js and browser-based development tools for building and testing the application.
  • WebAssembly, in optional experimental simulation features.
  • Git and GitHub for version control and public source-code hosting.
  • Cloudflare for deployment of the playable web application.
  • Browser storage for local saves and persistent project data.

The application is designed to run on ordinary computers and supported mobile browsers without requiring specialized gaming hardware.

Innovation and Creativity

MissionForge's primary innovation is connecting scientific objectives, spacecraft engineering, operational resource management, and educational explanations within a single playable experience.

Unlike a game focused solely on launching spacecraft, MissionForge encourages players to think about the complete mission lifecycle.

For example, selecting a more powerful scientific instrument may improve observation capability but also increase electricity consumption, storage requirements, spacecraft mass, and mission cost.

Likewise, a spacecraft can collect valuable scientific data but fail to return that information because its recorder fills up or its communication system cannot transmit enough data.

These interconnected trade-offs encourage experimentation, technical reasoning, and problem-solving.

Players can compare successful spacecraft designs to discover that a more expensive spacecraft is not always necessary to achieve an objective.

Testing and Validation

For the documented implementation revision, MissionForge successfully completed:

  • 378 core automated tests.
  • A strict production build.
  • Browser checks covering all three Mission Design Studio scenarios.
  • Checks for mobile portrait and landscape layouts.
  • Rocket-builder regression checks.
  • Verification of seven archived NASA source-file hashes.

These tests provide evidence of specific functionality and implementation reliability, but they do not establish that every possible gameplay configuration or device has been tested.

Intended Impact and Benefits

MissionForge aims to make space engineering more approachable for students, beginners, and people interested in astronomy or space exploration.

Its educational goals include helping players:

  • Understand how spacecraft design decisions influence mission outcomes.
  • Explore fundamental concepts such as orbital motion, propulsion, electricity generation, and communication.
  • Recognize the importance of balancing scientific objectives with engineering constraints.
  • Develop analytical thinking through experimentation and comparison.
  • Connect scientific concepts with practical, visible outcomes.

By making complex engineering decisions interactive, MissionForge seeks to encourage curiosity about space science, aerospace engineering, and STEM education.

Formal studies of its educational effectiveness have not yet been conducted.

Conclusion

MissionForge demonstrates how a browser-based game can combine NASA-derived scientific information, interactive engineering, mission operations, and educational feedback.

The project's central idea is simple:

Design a mission. Understand the trade-offs. Simulate the consequences. Learn from the results.

MissionForge turns space mission planning into an accessible, replayable learning experience.

Playable Project: https://mission-forge.pandeyshashankai.workers.dev/

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/pandeyshashankai/Mission-Forge
